title: Spelling Strategies
description: Spelling rules, patterns and memory strategies — homophones, common confusions and proofreading for spelling.

notes.heading: Why English Spelling Is Tricky
notes.body:
📌 Definition
English spelling is the system of written letters used to represent English words — and it is famously unreliable, because English has borrowed words from Latin, French, German, Norse and many other languages over more than a thousand years.

🔑 How it works
Because words arrived from so many different languages, the same sound can be spelled in several ways, and the same letters can be pronounced differently. Many words also contain silent letters that you cannot hear at all:
• silent vowels — friend (silent i)
• silent consonants — gnome (silent g), knife (silent k), island (silent s)
• squashed syllables — Wednesday is said "Wenz-day", chocolate is often "choc-late"

💡 Worked Example
Look at island. You never hear the s, so how would you guess it? A memory hook fixes it: an island is land surrounded by water — the word land is hiding inside it, and the s just comes along for the ride.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• English spelling does not always match pronunciation.
• Silent letters are common and must be memorised, not heard.
• Tricky words need strategies — mnemonics, sounding out, and word families — rather than guesswork.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Relying on "just sound it out" for every word. It works for some words, but it fails badly for island, knife, Wednesday and any homophone.

notes.heading: Mnemonics and Acrostics
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A mnemonic is any memory device that helps you remember something specific, such as the spelling of a word. An acrostic is a type of mnemonic: a phrase in which the first letters of each word spell out the tricky word itself.

🔑 How it works
You attach the difficult spelling to a sentence or image that is easy to recall. The sillier or more personal the hook, the better it sticks. You can invent your own for any word you keep getting wrong.

💡 Worked Example
Classic spelling mnemonics:
• because — Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants
• rhythm — Rhythm Helps Your Two Hips Move
• necessary — one collar, two sleeves (one c, two s's)
• separate — there is a rat in sep-a-rate
• their — it contains heir, a person who inherits possessions, so use it for possession

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Mnemonics work best for single words that break the usual rules.
• Acrostics use the first letters of a phrase to spell the word letter by letter.
• Build your own mnemonics for your personal problem words — self-made ones are remembered best.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Learning the mnemonic but not connecting it back to the word. Always write the word out straight after reciting the phrase so the two become linked.

notes.heading: Sounding Out — Say It As You Spell It
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Sounding out is the strategy of pronouncing a word the way it is written — exaggerating every syllable and silent letter — so the spelling becomes memorable.

🔑 How it works
1. Break the word into syllables.
2. Say each syllable exactly as it is spelled, even if that sounds wrong.
3. Write the word while repeating your exaggerated version.

💡 Worked Example
• cupboard — say cup-board (you never hear the p normally)
• believe — be-lie-ve, three clear beats
• environment — env-iron-ment, so you don't drop the middle n
• business — bus-i-ness, so you remember the i sits in the middle
• shepherd — shep-herd, like a person herding sheep
• Wednesday — Wed-nes-day, which rescues the silent first d

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Exaggerated pronunciation makes silent or squashed letters audible.
• Say it, then write it — the two together are stronger than either alone.
• This suits words where letters get swallowed in normal speech.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using sounding out on homophones. Their, there and they're all sound identical, so pronunciation alone can never tell you which spelling to use — that needs meaning-based hooks instead.

notes.heading: Homophones and Commonly Confused Words
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings and different spellings — for example their, there and they're.

🔑 How it works
Because the words sound identical, you must choose the spelling from meaning, not sound. Give each spelling its own memory hook:
• their shows possession — it hides the word heir, someone who inherits possessions: "The pupils forgot their books."
• there points to a place — it hides the word here: "Put it over there." Swapping in here still makes sense.
• they're is a contraction of they are — if you can replace it with they are, this is the one: "They're leaving soon."

💡 Worked Example
Other confusable pairs work the same way:
• your / you're — your shows possession; you're = you are
• its / it's — its shows possession; it's = it is or it has
• whose / who's — whose shows possession; who's = who is

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Test contractions by expanding them: if they are fits, write they're.
• For possession, look for the hidden word (heir in their) or no apostrophe at all (its, your, whose).
• Homophones are decided by meaning and grammar, never by sound.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing "The dog wagged it's tail." If you expand it to "The dog wagged it is tail" the sentence collapses — so the possessive its (no apostrophe) is correct.

✅ Check
Cover the sentence and say the expanded version aloud: they are, it is, you are, who is. If the expansion makes sense, keep the apostrophe; if not, use the possessive form.

notes.heading: Root Words, Prefixes and Suffixes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A root word is a base word that can grow into new words. A prefix is added to the front and a suffix to the end — each addition changes the meaning or the word class.

🔑 How it works
• Prefix + root: root becomes uproot; happy becomes unhappy.
• Root + suffix: root becomes rootless; care becomes careful.
• Both at once: happy becomes unhappily.

Knowing a root also unlocks meaning. The Latin port (carry) gives transport, import and portable; the Latin ducere (to lead) gives conductor and introduce.

💡 Worked Example
Even the longest words are just roots with parts bolted on. Antidisestablishmentarianism breaks into anti- (against) + dis- (opposite) + establish + -ment + -arian + -ism — a person opposed to the opposition to the establishment. Piece by piece, it is perfectly spellable.

Adding suffixes has its own spelling rules:
• Drop the silent e before a vowel suffix: hope → hoping, make → making.
• Keep the e before a consonant suffix: hope → hopeful, care → careless.
• Double the final consonant after a short vowel: run → running, big → biggest.
• Change y to i: happy → happily, beauty → beautiful.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Learn the spelling of a root word and you can spell the whole family grown from it.
• Prefixes rarely change the root's spelling: un- + happy = unhappy.
• Suffixes often do: watch for dropped e's, doubled consonants and y turning to i.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing runing or makeing. Check what the suffix starts with: a vowel suffix usually forces a change at the end of the root (drop the e or double the consonant).

notes.heading: Spelling Plural Nouns
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A plural noun names more than one of something. Most plurals follow regular spelling patterns, but a small group of irregular nouns must be learned individually.

🔑 How it works
• Most nouns: just add s — cat → cats, doughnut → doughnuts.
• Nouns ending in s, ss, sh, ch or x: add es — bus → buses, box → boxes, witch → witches.
• Nouns ending in consonant + o: usually add es — potato → potatoes, echo → echoes (but vowel + o just adds s: radio → radios, zoo → zoos).
• Nouns ending in consonant + y: drop the y and add ies — city → cities, sky → skies (but vowel + y just adds s: boy → boys, day → days).
• Nouns ending in f or fe: often change to ves — leaf → leaves, knife → knives.

💡 Worked Example
Irregular plurals break every pattern, so memorise them:
• man → men, woman → women
• child → children
• mouse → mice
• sheep → sheep, moose → moose (no change at all)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Check the letter before the final y or o — it decides whether you add s, es or ies.
• Endings s, sh, ch and x all take es because the extra e makes them pronounceable.
• Irregular plurals like children and mice are common words — learn them as vocabulary.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing citys or boyies. The rule depends on the letter before the y: consonant + y becomes ies (cities), but vowel + y keeps the y and just adds s (boys).

notes.heading: Proofreading for Spelling
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Proofreading is the final check of a piece of writing for errors, done after the content is finished. A spelling proofread means reading with one goal only: catching misspelled words.

🔑 How it works
• Proofread separately from editing — hunt spelling in its own pass, not while also fixing ideas.
• Slow down: point at each word, or read the text backwards word by word so meaning can't distract you.
• Keep a personal spelling list of words you have misspelled before, with a mnemonic for each.
• Check homophones deliberately — every their, your, its and who's deserves a second look.
• When unsure, use a dictionary rather than guessing.

💡 Worked Example
Draft sentence: "Their going to eat they're lunch over their."
Proofread with the expansion test and the place test:
• "Their going" → they are going, so write They're.
• "they're lunch" → possession, so write their.
• final "their" → a place (here/there), so write there.
Corrected: "They're going to eat their lunch over there."

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Spell-checkers miss wrong-but-real words: form instead of from, or their used for there.
• Your own error history is the best study guide — collect and drill your personal tricky words.
• Slow, single-purpose reading catches what fast reading slides over.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Trusting the spell-checker completely. It cannot tell you that "I went their yesterday" is wrong, because their is a perfectly good word — just the wrong one for that sentence.

flashcards.definition: A memory device that helps you remember something specific, such as how to spell a tricky word.
flashcards.example: "One collar, two sleeves" reminds you necessary has one c and two s's.

flashcards.definition: A mnemonic phrase in which the first letters of each word spell out the word you want to remember.
flashcards.example: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants spells BECAUSE.

flashcards.definition: A letter in a word's spelling that is not pronounced, so it must be memorised rather than heard.
flashcards.example: The s in island, the g in gnome and the k in knife are all silent.

flashcards.definition: A word that sounds the same as another word but has a different meaning and spelling.
flashcards.example: Their, there and they're are homophones — choose by meaning, not sound.

flashcards.definition: their = possession (contains heir); there = place (contains here); they're = they are.
flashcards.example: They're going to leave their coats over there.

flashcards.definition: Pronouncing a word exactly as it is spelled — exaggerating every syllable — to make the spelling stick.
flashcards.example: Saying env-iron-ment stops you writing enviroment and dropping the n.

flashcards.definition: A base word that can grow into new words when prefixes or suffixes are added.
flashcards.example: Root grows into uproot, rootless and rooted.

flashcards.definition: A word part added to the front of a root word to change its meaning.
flashcards.example: Un- + happy = unhappy; re- + write = rewrite.

flashcards.definition: A word part added to the end of a root word, often changing its meaning or word class.
When a suffix starting with a vowel is added to a word ending in silent e, drop the e.
In a short word ending in a single vowel plus single consonant, double the final consonant before a vowel suffix.
For a noun ending in a consonant plus y, change the y to i and add es; after a vowel plus y, just add s.
flashcards.example: City → cities and sky → skies, but boy → boys and day → days.

choices: A word with a silent letter
A memory device that helps you remember something, such as a spelling
A word that sounds like another word
questions.explanation: A mnemonic is any trick — a phrase, image or pattern — that makes something easier to remember, like a tricky spelling. The m is silent, fittingly.

questions.stem: Which acrostic correctly helps you spell BECAUSE?
choices: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants
Brave Eagles Can Always Use Small Exits
Big Ants Crawl Around Under Sweet Elderflowers
Brown Elephants Carry All Umbrellas Sometimes
questions.explanation: The first letters of Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants give B-E-C-A-U-S-E. The other phrases produce the wrong letter sequences.

questions.stem: Which word contains a silent consonant?
questions.explanation: Gnome begins with a silent g — you only hear "nome". Every letter in table, garden and rabbit is pronounced.

questions.stem: "___ going to the cinema after school." Which spelling completes the sentence?
questions.explanation: The sentence means "they are going", and they're is the contraction of they are. Their shows possession and there points to a place, so neither fits.

choices: The students left there homework in class.
Put the box over there by the door.
There going to win the match.
My friends have finished there project.
questions.explanation: There points to a place — it hides the word here — so it fits "over there". The other sentences need their (possession) or they're (they are).

questions.stem: What is the correct plural of "city"?
questions.explanation: City ends in consonant + y, so the y changes to i and es is added: cities. Just adding s (citys) is the classic error.

questions.stem: What is the correct plural of "box"?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in x take es to make them pronounceable, so box becomes boxes — the same pattern as bus → buses and witch → witches.

questions.stem: What is the correct plural of "potato"?
questions.explanation: Potato ends in consonant + o, so it takes es: potatoes, like echo → echoes. Nouns ending in vowel + o, such as radio, only add s.

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct plural?
choices: I saw five sheeps in the field.
I saw five sheep in the field.
I saw five sheepes in the field.
I saw five sheepies in the field.
questions.explanation: Sheep is an irregular noun that does not change in the plural — one sheep, five sheep. Moose behaves the same way.

questions.stem: What is the correct plural of "child"?
questions.explanation: Child has the irregular plural children, which already ends in the plural marker -en, so childrens adds a second, wrong plural.

questions.stem: Add the suffix -ing to "hope". What is the correct spelling?
questions.explanation: The suffix -ing starts with a vowel, so the silent e at the end of hope is dropped: hoping. Keeping the e would give the misspelling hopeing.

questions.stem: Add the suffix -ing to "run". What is the correct spelling?
questions.explanation: Run is a short word ending in single vowel + single consonant, so the n doubles before a vowel suffix: running — the same pattern as big → biggest.
The correct spelling is believe. Sounding it out as be-lie-ve helps you hear the ie order and remember all three syllables.

questions.stem: In "transport", "import" and "portable", the Latin root "port" means:
questions.explanation: Port means carry: transport carries things across, import carries them in, and something portable can be carried. To lead is the root ducere, as in conductor.

questions.stem: Why can't a spell-checker fully replace proofreading?
choices: Because spell-checkers are always switched off
Because a misspelled word that is still a real word — like "form" for "from" or "their" for "there" — will not be flagged
Because spell-checkers only work on printed text
Because proofreading is faster than using a spell-checker
questions.explanation: A spell-checker only spots words that do not exist. Their, form and from are all real words, so using the wrong one passes silently — only a careful human read catches it.
